title: Circle Geometry 1: Chords, Angles and Cyclic Quadrilaterals

topics.title: Arcs and angles at the centre

inlines.text: applies deductive reasoning to prove circle theorems and solve related problems
Prove and apply angle and chord properties of circles
Apply terminology associated with angles in circles
Identify the arc on which an angle at the centre or circumference stands
Demonstrate that at any point on a circle there is a unique tangent to the circle, and that this tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact
Apply chord and angle properties of circles to find unknown angles and lengths in diagrams
Prove and apply tangent and secant properties of circles
Prove tangent and secant properties of circles
Apply tangent and secant properties of circles to find unknown angles and lengths in diagrams
The circumference of a circle is the perimeter, or distance around the outside of a circle.
An arc is a continuous part of the circumference.
The centre is the point that is the same distance from every point on the circumference.
A circle is the set of all points an equal distance from the centre.
A tangent is a straight line that touches the circumference at a single point without entering the circle.
A chord is a straight line segment that goes from one point on the circumference to another point.

answer.short: $\angle ODQ$; $DO$; radii; AAS; matching sides in congruent triangles are equal.
answer.worked: $\angle OPB=\angle OQD=90^\circ$ (given). Since $P$ lies on $AB$ and $Q$ lies on $CD$, part a gives $\angle OBP=\angle ODQ$. Also $BO=DO$ (radii). Therefore $\triangle OPB\equiv\triangle OQD$ (AAS), so $OP=OQ$ (matching sides in congruent triangles are equal).

inlines.text: The perpendicular drawn from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.

spec.description: Sloping chord AB and dashed perpendicular OP. Radii OA and OB are intentionally absent.
spec.mathematics: O is the circle centre. A and B lie on the circle. P is the perpendicular foot on chord AB.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied chord, dashed perpendicular, right-angle marker, centre dot and labels are visible.

answer.worked:
In $\triangle OAP$ and $\triangle OBP$:

$$\begin{aligned}\angle OPA&=\angle OPB=90^\circ\\OA&=OB\end{aligned}$$

The angles are right angles because $OP\perp AB$, and $OA=OB$ because they are radii. Also $OP$ is common.

Therefore $\triangle OAP\equiv\triangle OBP$ (RHS). Hence $AP=PB$ (corresponding sides of congruent triangles are equal). The perpendicular drawn from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.

content.prompt:
In this diagram, radius $AD=5\text{ mm}$, radius $BD=12\text{ mm}$ and chord $CD=8\text{ mm}$.

spec.description: Smaller circle centred at A on the left and larger circle centred at B on the right. C and D are their upper and lower intersections. Solid line AB crosses dashed common chord CD; all four radii to the intersections are dashed.
spec.mathematics: AD = AC = 5 mm; BD = BC = 12 mm; CD = 8 mm. The centres lie on opposite sides of the common chord. Coordinates derive from half-chord 4 mm, with distances 3 mm and 8√2 mm from the common chord.
spec.answerVisibility: The diagram contains only the source labels A, B, C and D. No numerical result or added midpoint label appears.

answer.worked:
Let $M$ be the intersection of $AB$ and $CD$. The line joining the centres bisects the common chord at right angles, so $DM=4\text{ mm}$.
$$\begin{aligned}AM^2&=AD^2-DM^2\\AM^2&=5^2-4^2=9\\AM&=3\text{ mm}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}BM^2&=BD^2-DM^2\\BM^2&=12^2-4^2=128\\BM&=8\sqrt{2}\text{ mm}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}AB&=AM+BM\\AB&=(3+8\sqrt{2})\text{ mm}\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt: Find the exact length of $PQ$, in surd form.

answer.worked:
Let $M$ be the intersection of $PQ$ and $XY$. The line joining the centres bisects the common chord at right angles, so $XM=6\text{ cm}$.
$$\begin{align*}PM^2&=PX^2-XM^2\\PM^2&=10^2-6^2=64\\PM&=8\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}QM^2&=QX^2-XM^2\\QM^2&=9^2-6^2=45\\QM&=3\sqrt{5}\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}PQ&=PM+QM\\PQ&=(8+3\sqrt{5})\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

answer.short: Base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal (equal radii); $\angle OAC$; $\angle OCA$; $x+y$.
answer.worked:
Since $OA=OC$, the base angles of $\triangle AOC$ are equal.
$$\begin{align*}\angle OAC&=\angle OCA=x\\\angle POA&=\angle OAC+\angle OCA\\\angle POA&=2x\end{align*}$$
Similarly, $OB=OC$ gives $\angle POB=2y$ by the exterior-angle property.
$$\begin{align*}\angle AOB&=2x+2y\\\angle AOB&=2(x+y)\\\angle AOB&=2\times\angle ACB\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Centre outside angle ACB; dashed diameter POC, equal-radius double ticks, x between CA and CO and y spanning CO to CB.
spec.mathematics: OA=OB; P,O,C are collinear. Angle ACB=y-x; y is the entire angle OCB.
spec.answerVisibility: No completed proof or derived angle values.

answer.worked:
Equal radii give equal base angles in $\triangle AOC$ and $\triangle BOC$. By the exterior-angle property,
$$\begin{align*}\angle POA&=x+x\\\angle POA&=2x\\\angle POB&=y+y\\\angle POB&=2y\\\angle AOB&=\angle POB-\angle POA\\\angle AOB&=2y-2x\\\angle AOB&=2(y-x)\end{align*}$$
At $C$, $\angle ACB=y-x$. Therefore $\angle AOB=2\times\angle ACB$.

answer.short: The angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc; $180$; angles on a straight line equal $180^\circ$; $180$.

children.prompt: Explain why “The angle in a semicircle is $90^\circ$” is a special case of “The angle at the centre of a circle is twice the angle at the circumference when standing on the same arc.”

answer.short: A diameter gives an angle of $180^\circ$ at the centre, so the angle at the circumference is $180^\circ\div2=90^\circ$.
answer.worked: When $AB$ is a diameter, $\angle AOB=180^\circ$. The angle at the circumference standing on the same semicircular arc is half this angle, so $\angle ACB=90^\circ$.

spec.mathematics: The angle ACB is 32° and O is the centre.

answer.worked:
The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc.
$$\begin{align*}\angle AOB &= 2\times32^\circ\\&=64^\circ\end{align*}$$
Since $OA=OB$, triangle $AOB$ is isosceles.
$$\begin{align*}\angle OAB &= \frac{180^\circ-64^\circ}{2}\\&=58^\circ\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle ACB &=12^\circ+25^\circ\\&=37^\circ\\\angle AOB &=2\times37^\circ\\&=74^\circ\end{align*}$$
The centre angle is twice the circumference angle on the same arc. Since $OA=OB$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle OAB &=\frac{180^\circ-74^\circ}{2}\\&=53^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Triangle with an unlabelled upper-right vertex, radii OB and OA, and external 18° and 21° pointers.
spec.mathematics: The given angles are between OB and the upper chord at B, and between OA and the upper chord at A.
spec.answerVisibility: The upper-right point has no printed label; no answer is shown.

answer.worked:
Let $P$ be the unlabelled point. Since $OB=OP$ and $OA=OP$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle BPO &=18^\circ\\\angle OPA &=21^\circ\\\angle BPA &=18^\circ+21^\circ\\&=39^\circ\\\angle BOA &=2\times39^\circ\\&=78^\circ\end{align*}$$
Since $OA=OB$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle OAB &=\frac{180^\circ-78^\circ}{2}\\&=51^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Triangle with unlabelled bottom vertex, radii OA and OB, 19° at A and 26° at B.
spec.mathematics: The 19° and 26° givens lie between each radius and the chord to the bottom point.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied angles are shown.

answer.worked:
Let $P$ be the unlabelled bottom point. Since $OA=OP$ and $OB=OP$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle APO &=19^\circ\\\angle OPB &=26^\circ\\\angle APB &=19^\circ+26^\circ\\&=45^\circ\\\angle AOB &=2\times45^\circ\\&=90^\circ\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
Let $D$ be the unlabelled circumference point and $X$ the crossing. The centre angle is twice the circumference angle on arc $AD$.
$$\begin{align*}\angle AOD &=2\times48^\circ\\&=96^\circ\end{align*}$$
Vertically opposite angles give $\angle AXO=65^\circ$. Since $X$ lies on $OD$ and $AB$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle OAB &=180^\circ-96^\circ-65^\circ\\&=19^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Two chords from B, radii to A and the unlabelled upper-left point, and external 57° and 36° pointers.
spec.mathematics: The angle between the upper-left radius and its chord to B is 57°; the angle between the two chords at B is 36°.
spec.answerVisibility: The upper-left point remains unlabelled; only givens are shown.

answer.worked:
Let $P$ be the unlabelled upper-left point. Since $OP=OB$, $\angle PBO=57^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\angle POB &=180^\circ-2\times57^\circ\\&=66^\circ\\\angle POA &=2\times36^\circ\\&=72^\circ\\\angle BOA &=66^\circ+72^\circ\\&=138^\circ\end{align*}$$
The angle $POA$ is twice the circumference angle $PBA$. Since $OA=OB$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle OAB &=\frac{180^\circ-138^\circ}{2}\\&=21^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.mathematics: CBP is straight and opposite cyclic angles ABC and ADC are supplementary.
spec.answerVisibility: x is the supplied proof variable; no completed responses in the figure.

answer.short: $180^\circ-x$; $x$; opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.
answer.worked:
Let $\angle ABP=x$.
$$\angle ABC=180^\circ-x$$
($CBP$ is a straight line.)
$$\begin{aligned}\angle ADC&=180^\circ-(180^\circ-x)\\\angle ADC&=x\end{aligned}$$
(Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.)
$$\therefore\ \angle ABP=\angle ADC.$$

The points $A$, $B$ and $C$ lie on a circle with centre $O$, as shown in the diagram.

What is the size of $\angle ABC$ in radians?

(B) $\frac{2\pi}{5}$
(C) $\frac{7\pi}{10}$

answer.worked:
The angle at the circumference is half the angle at the centre on the same arc.
The arc $AC$ that $\angle ABC$ stands on is the major arc, so use reflex $\angle AOC$.
$$\begin{align*}
\text{reflex } \angle AOC &= 2\pi - \frac{3\pi}{5} \\
&= \frac{7\pi}{5} \\
\angle ABC &= \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{7\pi}{5} \\
&= \frac{7\pi}{10}
\end{align*}$$
The answer is (C).

content.prompt:
The circle centred at $O$ with radius $r$ has a diameter $AB$.
Points $C$ and $D$ are chosen on the circle as shown in the diagram.
The chord $AC$ has length $d$.
Show that $d=2r\sin D$.

answer.short: Proof: $\angle ABC=\angle ADC=D$ and $\angle ACB=90^\circ$, so $\sin D=\dfrac{d}{2r}$ and $d=2r\sin D$.
answer.worked:
Angles subtended by the same arc $AC$ at the circumference are equal:
$$\begin{align*}
\angle ABC &= \angle ADC = D
\end{align*}$$
The angle in a semi-circle is a right angle, so in $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{align*}
\angle ACB &= 90^\circ
\end{align*}$$
Using right-angled trigonometry in $\triangle ABC$, where the hypotenuse is the diameter $AB = 2r$ and the side opposite to $\angle ABC$ is $AC = d$:
$$\begin{align*}
\sin(\angle ABC) &= \frac{\text{Opposite}}{\text{Hypotenuse}} \\
\sin D &= \frac{d}{2r} \\
d &= 2r \sin D
\end{align*}$$

Let $\angle XDP=\alpha$.

answer.worked:
From part (i), $\triangle BQX$ is isosceles, so $QB=QX$.
In $\triangle BXC$, $\angle XCB=90^\circ-\angle XBC$, and $\angle QXC=90^\circ-\angle QXB$.
Since $\angle QXB=\angle XBC$, we have $\angle QXC=\angle XCB$, so $QC=QX$.
Therefore $QB=QC$, so $Q$ bisects $BC$.

content.prompt:
The diagram shows quadrilateral $ABCD$ and the bisectors of the angles at $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$. The bisectors at $A$ and $B$ intersect at the point $P$. The bisectors at $A$ and $D$ meet at $Q$. The bisectors at $C$ and $D$ meet at $R$. The bisectors at $B$ and $C$ meet at $S$.

Show that $PQRS$ is a cyclic quadrilateral.

spec.description: Quadrilateral and its four angle bisectors, with Q below BC and the inner quadrilateral emphasised.
spec.mathematics: P=AP∩BP, Q=AQ∩DQ, R=CR∩DR, S=BS∩CS; each vertex angle has two equal labelled halves.
spec.answerVisibility: All supplied angle-half labels are permanent givens; the proof is answer-only.

answer.worked:
Let $\alpha=\frac12\angle A$, $\beta=\frac12\angle B$, $\gamma=\frac12\angle C$ and $\delta=\frac12\angle D$.

The angle sum of quadrilateral $ABCD$ gives
$$\begin{align*}2\alpha+2\beta+2\gamma+2\delta&=360^\circ\\\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta&=180^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Using the angle sums of $\triangle BSC$ and $\triangle AQD$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle PSR&=\angle BSC=180^\circ-(\beta+\gamma)\\\angle PQR&=\angle AQD=180^\circ-(\alpha+\delta).\end{align*}$$
Here $SP$ lies along $SB$ and $SR$ lies along $SC$, while $QP$ lies along $QA$ and $QR$ lies along $QD$.
$$\begin{align*}\angle PSR+\angle PQR&=2\times180^\circ-(\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta)\\\angle PSR+\angle PQR&=2\times180^\circ-180^\circ\\\angle PSR+\angle PQR&=180^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $PQRS$ is cyclic because its opposite angles are supplementary.

As $\triangle ADB$ is isosceles (with $AD=BD$), $\angle DAB = \angle ABD = x$.
The exterior angle of $\triangle ABD$ is $\angle ADC = x + x = 2x$.
So $\angle ADC = 2x = \angle AOC$.

children.prompt:
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AC$ and $P$ the centre of the circle through $A$, $C$, $D$ and $O$.
Show that $P$, $M$ and $O$ are collinear.

answer.worked:
$AC$ is a chord of the circle passing through $A, C, D, O$. The centre of this circle is $P$. The line joining the centre of a circle ($P$) to the midpoint ($M$) of a chord ($AC$) is perpendicular to the chord.
Similarly, in the original circle with centre $O$, $AC$ is a chord and $M$ is its midpoint, so $OM$ is perpendicular to $AC$.
Since both $PM$ and $OM$ are perpendicular to $AC$ at the same point $M$, the points $P$, $M$, and $O$ must lie on the same straight line. Thus they are collinear.

answer.short: $CMDE$ is cyclic because exterior $\angle ACB$ equals opposite interior $\angle MDE$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle ADB&=90^\circ\\\angle BCA&=90^\circ\end{align*}$$
Both are angles in a semicircle. Since $DB$ and $DM$ are opposite rays, and $DE$ lies along $DA$,
$$\angle MDE=180^\circ-\angle ADB=90^\circ.$$
Thus exterior $\angle ACB$ equals opposite interior $\angle MDE$, so $CMDE$ is cyclic.

children.prompt: Hence, or otherwise, prove that $MF$ is perpendicular to $AB$.

answer.worked:
Construct $CD$. Let $\angle ABC=x$.

Angles standing on chord $AC$ give $\angle ADC=x$. Since $D,E,A$ are collinear, $\angle EDC=x$. In cyclic quadrilateral $CMDE$, angles standing on chord $CE$ give $\angle CME=\angle CDE=x$.

In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle BCA=90^\circ$, so
$$\angle CAB=90^\circ-x.$$
Since $MC$ lies along $MA$ and $ME$ lies along $MF$, the angle sum of $\triangle MFA$ gives
$$\begin{align*}\angle MFA&=180^\circ-\angle CME-\angle CAB\\\angle MFA&=180^\circ-x-(90^\circ-x)\\\angle MFA&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $MF\perp AB$.

content.prompt:
In the acute-angled triangle $ABC$, $K$ is the midpoint of $AB$, $L$ is the midpoint of $BC$ and $M$ is the midpoint of $CA$.
The circle through $K$, $L$ and $M$ also cuts $BC$ at $P$ as shown in the diagram.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Prove that $KMLB$ is a parallelogram.

answer.short: $KM\parallel BL$ and $KM=BL$, so $KMLB$ is a parallelogram.
answer.worked:
In $\triangle ABC$, $K$ and $M$ are midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$, so $KM\parallel BC$ and $KM=\frac{1}{2}BC$.
$L$ is the midpoint of $BC$, so $BL=\frac{1}{2}BC$.
Thus $KM\parallel BL$ and $KM=BL$.
One pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel, so $KMLB$ is a parallelogram.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Prove that $\angle KPB = \angle KML$.

answer.short: Exterior angle of cyclic quadrilateral $KMLP$ equals the interior opposite angle.
answer.worked:
$KMLP$ is a cyclic quadrilateral, since $K$, $M$, $L$, $P$ lie on the circle.
The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle.
Therefore $\angle KPB=\angle KML$.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Prove that $AP \perp BC$.

answer.short: $KP=KA=KB$, so $P$ lies on the circle with diameter $AB$, and $\angle APB=90^\circ$.
answer.worked:
Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, so $\angle KML=\angle KBL$.
From part (ii), $\angle KPB=\angle KML=\angle KBP$.
So $\triangle KBP$ is isosceles with $KP=KB$.
$K$ is the midpoint of $AB$, so $KB=KA$, giving $KP=KA=KB$.
Thus $P$ lies on the circle with diameter $AB$, and the angle in a semicircle is $90^\circ$.
So $\angle APB=90^\circ$ and $AP\perp BC$.

spec.description: Acute triangle ABC with the circle through the midpoints K (on AB), L (on BC), M (on CA). The circle also cuts BC at P. Points K, L, M, P are labelled.
spec.mathematics: K, L, M are midpoints of AB, BC, CA. The circle through K, L, M passes through P on BC, the foot of the altitude from A (the nine-point circle). Coordinates: B(0,0), C(4.85,0), A(1.33,2.86), circle centre (1.8775,1.1241), radius 1.2504.
spec.answerVisibility: No parallelogram, equal-length marks or right-angle marks; AP and KP are not drawn.

content.prompt:
In the diagram $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral.
The point $K$ is on $AC$ such that $\angle ADK = \angle CDB$, and hence $\triangle ADK$ is similar to $\triangle BDC$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that $\triangle ADB$ is similar to $\triangle KDC$.

answer.worked:
In $\triangle ADB$ and $\triangle KDC$:
$\angle ADB = \angle ADK + \angle KDB = \angle CDB + \angle KDB = \angle KDC$ (given)
$\angle ABD = \angle KCD$ (angles in the same segment)
$\therefore \triangle ADB \sim \triangle KDC$ (equiangular)

children.label: b
children.prompt: Using the fact that $AC = AK + KC$, show that $BD \times AC = AD \times BC + AB \times DC$.

children.label: c
children.prompt:
A regular pentagon of side length $1$ is inscribed in a circle, as shown in the diagram.
Let $x$ be the length of a chord in the pentagon.
Use the result in part (b) to show that $x = \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$.

content.prompt: In this circle $\angle BAO=\angle CAO$. Prove $AB=AC$. Suggestion: Construct $BC$.

spec.description: Circle with centre O, top point A, lower circumference points B and C, chords AB and AC, and a vertical diameter through A and O. Matching angle arcs and filled dots mark the two equal angles at A. BC is absent.
spec.mathematics: A, B and C lie on the circle; O is its centre; angle BAO equals angle CAO.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible. The requested construction BC and proof radii OB and OC are not supplied.

answer.worked:
Construct $BC$ and join $OB$ and $OC$.

$OA=OB=OC$ (radii), so $\triangle OAB$ and $\triangle OAC$ are isosceles. Thus $\angle ABO=\angle BAO$ and $\angle ACO=\angle CAO$.

Since $\angle BAO=\angle CAO$ (given), $\angle ABO=\angle ACO$. Also, $OA$ is common.

Therefore, $\triangle OAB\cong\triangle OAC$ (AAS), so $AB=AC$ (corresponding sides).

content.prompt: Find the values of the pronumerals.

spec.description: Cyclic quadrilateral with both diagonals, extensions of its lower side beyond both endpoints, and x in the intersection sector towards the left and bottom-left vertices. Vertex names used internally are not printed.
spec.mathematics: Internal vertices A, B, C, D run from left to top to right-lower to bottom-left. Angle BAC is 50 degrees. Exterior angles at D and C are 82 and 106 degrees respectively. E is the intersection of AC and BD; x is angle AED.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the source givens 50°, 82°, 106° and pronumeral x are visible; the supplied answer is omitted.

answer.worked:
Call the left, top, right-lower and bottom-left vertices $A,B,C,D$, respectively, and the diagonal intersection $E$.

The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the opposite interior angle. Hence $\angle BAD=106^\circ$. Angles standing on the same arc give $\angle BDC=50^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}
\angle DAE&=106^\circ-50^\circ\\
&=56^\circ\\
\angle ADC&=180^\circ-82^\circ\\
&=98^\circ\\
\angle ADE&=98^\circ-50^\circ\\
&=48^\circ\\
x&=180^\circ-56^\circ-48^\circ\\
&=76^\circ
\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.method: Angles at the circumference standing on the same arc are equal.
An exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the opposite interior angle.

content.prompt: In this question we will prove the following theorem. When two circles intersect, the line joining their centres bisects that common chord at right angles.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Prove $\triangle ACD\cong\triangle BCD$.

spec.description: Two intersecting circles, with the left circle larger. Centres C and D lie on CD. Intersections B above and A below are joined by the common chord AB, meeting CD at E. All four radii CA, CB, DA and DB are drawn. The figure is shared by parts a–c.
spec.mathematics: CA=CB and DA=DB are radii of their respective circles. E is the intersection of AB and CD. Construction coordinates determine the circle intersections; no numerical measurements are printed.
spec.answerVisibility: No perpendicularity mark, bisection ticks or congruence annotations are supplied.

answer.worked:
$AD=BD$ (radii of the circle with centre $D$).

$AC=BC$ (radii of the circle with centre $C$).

$CD$ is common.

Therefore, $\triangle ACD\cong\triangle BCD$ (SSS).

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, prove $\triangle ACE\cong\triangle BCE$.

answer.worked:
$AC=BC$ (radii).

$\angle ACE=\angle BCE$ (corresponding angles in the congruent triangles from part a, since $C,E,D$ are collinear).

$CE$ is common.

Therefore, $\triangle ACE\cong\triangle BCE$ (SAS).

children.label: c
children.prompt: Hence, prove $CD\perp AB$ and $BE=EA$.

answer.worked:
$\angle BEC=\angle CEA$ (corresponding angles in the congruent triangles from part b).

These angles lie on the straight line $AB$, so each is $90^\circ$. Therefore, $CD\perp AB$.

Also, $BE=EA$ (corresponding sides in $\triangle ACE\cong\triangle BCE$).

MA5-CIR-P-01 applies deductive reasoning to prove circle theorems and solve related problems

Prove and apply angle and chord properties of circles
• Apply terminology associated with angles in circles
• Identify the arc on which an angle at the centre or circumference stands
• Demonstrate that at any point on a circle there is a unique tangent to the circle, and that this tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact
• Prove chord properties of circles
• Prove angle properties of circles
• Apply chord and angle properties of circles to find unknown angles and lengths in diagrams

Prove and apply tangent and secant properties of circles
• Prove tangent and secant properties of circles
• Apply tangent and secant properties of circles to find unknown angles and lengths in diagrams

P, C and Q lie on the horizontal tangent at C, with P left and Q right. The tangent at A meets this line at Q and extends beyond A. Drawn segments include AB, BC, OC, AC, OQ, PQ and AQ. All point labels P, B, O, A, C, Q are visible. Single ticks mark OB, OA and OC; double ticks mark PB and BC; triple ticks mark AQ and CQ. Solution annotations show φ at ∠BPC, φ at ∠BCP, 2φ at ∠OBC, φ at ∠BAC, and a right-angle marker at ∠BCA.

entries.description: Supplied blue worked proof beneath the diagram.
entries.expectedAnswer:
Construct OC, AC, OQ.
Let ∠BPC have size φ.
△BPC is isosceles so ∠BCP is φ.
∠OBC is an external angle, so ∠OBC = 2φ.
∠BAC is angle on chord BC, so ∠BAC = φ (angle in alternate segment and angle between chord and tangent).
But △BAC has a right angle at C (angle in semicircle).
So φ + 2φ = 90°, hence φ = 30°.
OA ⟂ AQ (angle between tangent and radius).
So ∠CAQ = 60°.
QA = QC (tangents from point equal).
So ∠QCA = 60° (△QAC isosceles).
Hence ∠AQC = 60° (angle sum of triangle).
△OAQ and △OCQ are congruent (SSS: OA = OC, radii; AQ = CQ, above; OQ common).
So ∠OQC = 60°/2 = 30° = ∠OPC.
Thus △OPQ is isosceles, and OP = OQ.

presentation.answerPlacement: Worked-answer edition only; keep supplied proof and derived diagram annotations out of the student prompt.
presentation.taughtMethods: Isosceles triangles, exterior angle, alternate segment theorem, angle in a semicircle, tangent-radius perpendicularity, equal tangents, triangle angle sum and SSS congruence.
